Senses.Explanation: The Accord of Difference and Sameness is the title of Shitou Xiqian’s verse, identified as a composed work, quoted by its opening and closing lines, and discussed by later masters. The title combines participation or joining , sameness , and accord or tally . In the Chan corpus it is the proper name of Shitou Xiqian's verse. The Transmission of the Lamp says that Shitou wrote it, calls its language deep, and prints the work under his name. Its opening says that the mind of the great Indian immortal is intimately transmitted east and west ; its closing tells the person investigating the mystery to meet the source on hearing words and not waste the daylight . Fayan Wenyi later invokes the title in hall discourse, calls it a piece of wording, and quotes its opening. The Joint Essentials of the Lamps connects Shitou's composition with his reading that the sage has no self and nothing is not himself . Zen bends the phrase into a lineage-specific bibliographic name: these records use it not for a general agreement but for Shitou's transmitted Chan poem and for quotations from that poem.

To join, attend, or report to the communal hall. Biographical records use the expression for formal admission: people seeking to join the hall might wait for months, while a favored visitor is admitted that same day; Wuzu orders Yuanwu to join the hall immediately, after which Yuanwu enters the attendants' quarters. In encounter records the imperative 'go to the hall' regularly closes or dismisses an exchange. Wuju says it after striking two visitors, and Wenshu Siye shouts it to a former butcher, who then goes down to the hall. In commentary on the rhinoceros-fan case, an unnamed monk tells the entire assembly to go to the hall, and Yuanwu explicitly says that the unnamed monk has seized the authority of the host. The institutional and imperative uses share the same hall-directed action.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 529 matches in 137 files. The imperative 'go to the hall' accounts for 349 matches in 99 files, including seven matches in six files that address the whole assembly. The nominal form 'those who seek or attend the hall' occurs four times in four files; 'ordered him immediately to join the hall' occurs ten times in ten files, and 'then went down to the hall' occurs nineteen times in sixteen. These forms distinguish this institutional use of 'join' from other senses of the first graph elsewhere in Chan vocabulary.

Senses.Explanation: The formula records a claim that travel among teachers and inquiry have reached completion. Dunan Zongyan quotes and rejects an inherited claim that recognizing the staff finishes a lifetime's inquiry; Lingyan Chu, Chengshan Qia, Changqing Huileng, and Poshan Haiming each state conditions under which the inquiry is finished. The phrase marks a claimed verdict, not an automatic certificate attached to any strong answer.

The phrase names sustained investigation of Chan rather than merely learning information about it. Gaofeng Yuanmiao says that investigating Chan requires an iron person whose mind is decided on taking it up, calls the great matter of life and death its crucial point, and compares its aim of awakening with livelihood's aim of wealth. Zhongfeng Mingben criticizes people who speak of investigating Chan only with their mouths and turn encounter records into conversation material. Xueguan Zhiyin insists on determined effort rather than merely staring toward the school’s signboard. Dahui Zonggao retrospectively calls his own years before breakthrough investigation of Chan; Konggu Daocheng joins it to strenuous personal effort. An unnamed lay questioner asks Yongjue Yuanxian where investigating Chan gains force. Together these uses denote committed inquiry directed toward resolving the great matter, while warning that verbal cleverness does not constitute that inquiry.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 3,248 hits in 356 files and 353 works. Eight exact witnesses across six independent works cover required disposition, aim, life-and-death scope, verbal counterfeit, puzzle, autobiography, effort, and interview use.

Senses.Explanation: To investigate the particular word, saying, question, or conversational thread singled out from a recorded exchange. Frozen-corpus concordance: 195 exact hits in 81 storage files representing 81 independent works. Poshan Haiming identifies what remains unresolved in a scripture or public case as one's personally investigated saying. Zhongfeng Mingben supplies the actual question, 'Why did Zhaozhou say the word no?', and directs the listener to investigate that wording and raise great doubt. Zhanran Yuancheng says to investigate one's own selected saying in earnest, while Ruibai Mingxue says to place it before one and keep it continually in mind. Other witnesses explicitly police the action: Zhuanyu Heng criticizes seeking the wording in books and other people's mouths and asks whether those who perform it differ from those who do not; Zongbao Daodu says earlier patriarchs did not teach people to investigate sayings and presents the instruction as a later response to proliferating calculations; Gumei You says not to speculate over public cases or search in scriptures. Zen bends recorded public speech into the selected object of investigation, while the same records challenge where the wording is sought, what the action is taken to accomplish, and whether it should be reified.

A visit to a named instructor or assembly in order to ask questions and request instruction. It occurs 243 times in 121 allowlisted texts and includes both institutional attendance and the encounter itself. Zhicheng leaves Shenxiu, travels to Shaoyang, and "joins the assembly to visit and inquire" (隨眾參請); Shuangfeng Gu's biography says that at Shishuang he merely followed the assembly and "no longer visited and inquired" (更不參請). The monastic regulations place "traveling from place to place to visit and inquire" (遊方參請) under a heading that lists departure from one's teacher, seeking a respected elder, requesting lodging, first reporting to the guest office, and next registering at the hall office. Huanyuan Fuyu "bent his knees to visit and inquire" (屈膝參請), after which Lingyin Tai addressed his understanding. Tianning's monastic and lay followers visited and inquired morning and evening while Huqiu Shaolong answered them without weariness (晨夕參請，師與唱酬無倦). The recorded actions are visits, institutional participation, questions, and responses in Chinese Chan texts.
Senses.Note: Productive constructions mark the same range: "join the assembly to visit and inquire" (隨眾參請, 23 occurrences), "enter the room to visit and inquire" (入室參請, 2), "travel from place to place to visit and inquire" (遊方參請, 6), and headings for "circumstances of visiting and inquiry" (參請因緣, 2). Fayan can ask what scripture someone reads "apart from visiting and inquiry" (於參請外), placing it among the ordinary activities of a visitor's life. The Blue Cliff Record contrasts a superintendent's not having "visited and inquired or entered the room" (不曾參請入室) with Fayan subsequently asking why he does not come enter the room. The overlap between travel, residence in an assembly, and direct exchange is native to the term, so these are kept as deployments of one sense.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the lineage seal transmitted and applied to mind
Senses.Explanation: A lineage seal said to be transmitted from teacher to heir and applied to mind: the records preserve stamp grammar rather than a physical object. The term occurs 1,374 times in 280 allowed texts. Chuming Baoyin says the ancestral mind-seal is neither long nor short, square nor round, inside nor outside, nor in between (祖師心印，非長非短，非方非圓，非內非外，亦非中間). Jingjie Shoumi says it has no trace or shape and remains distinct and uninterrupted through the ages (祖師心印，無痕無狀。歷劫分明，未嘗間斷). Fengxue Yanzhao compares it to the mechanism of an iron ox: 'going, it seals and holds; staying, it seals and breaks' (去即印住。住即印破). Shishuang Chuyuan says one seal imprints empty space, water, and mud (一印印空。一印印水。一印印泥). Huangbo Xiyun says Bodhidharma 'secretly transmitted the mind-seal, imprinting your original mind; mind imprints the teaching, and the teaching imprints mind' (密傳心印，印你本心。以心印法，以法印心). Sengna says the ancestral mind-seal does not consist exclusively in harsh conduct (祖師心印非專苦行), while Weishan Huaixiu says the mind-seal of buddhas and ancestors is known only through confirmation (佛祖心印，唯證乃知). These are the corpus's formal, material, and transmission predicates; they do not turn the seal into a literal implement.
Senses.Note: Required definition formulas found no single prose gloss of the bare compound, but several direct shape-negations and seal-mechanism explanations. 'Ancestral mind-seal' (祖師心印) occurs 336 times in 145 texts, while 'mind-seal of buddhas and ancestors' occurs 23 times in 17. Proper-name uses belong to the separate personal-title sense below.

Senses.Explanation: Here the graph translated as "thing" or "what is established" (法) is contextual: in the recurring pair "this thing is mind; outside mind no thing stands; this mind is the thing; outside it no mind stands" (此法即心，心外無法；此心即法，法外無心), it names what could be set up as a thing apart, not an untranslated religious loanword. Shao's frequently quoted verse places the phrase beside visible landscape: "the summit of Tongxuan is not the human world; outside mind no thing stands; blue mountains fill the eyes" (通玄峰頂，不是人間；心外無法，滿目青山). A later master quotes that verse and says it has been "broken into two pieces" (打成兩橛). Another hall address strikes the Chan seat and asks: "mind has not arisen—where could the things be established? Where did mountains, rivers, and the great earth come from?" (心既不生，法從何立？山河大地，甚處得來). The corpus therefore records the line as a maxim, a verse, a question to the assembly, and an object of later criticism; this entry does not decide the criticism.

Senses.Explanation: The place of mental activity ceasing is a formula for thought no longer having a place to proceed; the records state it, question it, and sometimes put it in a rejected explanation. The standard companion is "the road of language is cut off" (言語道斷, 171 occurrences). A transmission record explains the parallel syntax: "when principle is clear, the road of language is cut off—what words could discuss it? When the purport is met, the place of mental activity is extinguished—what contemplation could think it?" (理明則言語道斷，何言之能議；旨會則心行處滅，何觀之能思). Hongzhi asks, "just when the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished, what then?" (言語道斷心行處滅，又作麼生). A later address quotes "it cannot be known by wisdom or recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off, the place of mental activity extinguished," then answers with a deliberate counter-formulation: "it can also be known by wisdom and recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off, mental activity is not extinguished" (心行不滅). Zhongfeng also reports an interpreter's equation: "cut off thought, then the place of mental activity is extinguished" (絕慮則心行處滅), before contesting that line of equation in the following passage. The entry therefore records the fixed pair, explicit parallel, question, and counter-witness rather than equating the phrase with blankness.

Senses.Explanation: The Yellow Emperor is the ancient ruler whom Chan records invoke through visits to recluses, the south-pointing carriage, and the lost pearl at Red Water. Wansong recounts his battle with Chiyou: Chiyou makes a great fog, and the emperor’s south-pointing carriage guides the troops. The Yongzheng Emperor invokes Huangdi visiting Guangchengzi to ask about the Way as a precedent for rulers seeking instruction. Shiyu Mingfang raises the story in which Huangdi loses the bright pearl at Red Water and Wangxiang recovers it, then uses the story inside a public question about truth, falsity, concealment, and manifestation. Juelang Daosheng places him among the sage rulers whom Zhuangzi’s writing both deploys and undercuts. The Zen Yellow Emperor is therefore the named ruler as masters quote and reposition him, not an imported general biography.

SearchAliases: the dream while the yellow millet cooked
Senses.Explanation: Yellow millet names the dream-meal allusion that Chan records invoke for a grand career experienced while the millet cooks. The primary Chan deployment is the yellow-millet dream, in which a lifetime of rank and glory passes during the time the millet takes to cook. Baichi Xingyuan's recorded sayings supply the story's frame directly: Lu's Handan pillow contains fifty years of glory, but when he wakes, the yellow millet is still not cooked (邯鄲一枕，歷盡榮華五十載，覺來黃粱炊尚未熟, “on one Handan pillow he passed through fifty years of glory; on waking, the yellow millet was still not cooked”). The allusion then enters public exchange and formal address. Tian'an Sheng answers, “when the yellow-millet dream breaks, one knows it is dawn” (黃粱夢破知天曉), and rejects the student's follow-up as more sleep-talk. Sanyi Yu places bells and pipes beside “waking from the yellow millet” (黃粱喚醒) before selling Yunmen's flatbread at the crossroads. Yunxi Langting Ting calls dream-life a gathering of sleepers and verses that “on one awakening, the yellow millet is cooked” (一覺黃粱熟). The Chan-specific bend is this use of an ordinary grain and its cooking time as the name and timing-device of a repeatedly quoted dream allusion; the entry does not decide what any master intended beyond the recorded comparisons.

Senses.Note: The ordinary-grain witness is retained to prevent the much richer dream family from absorbing every bare occurrence automatically.
